edits.find:
Acute low back pain, no red flag, normal neurologic exam: no imaging; an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) or acetaminophen, and stay active Why no imagingDisc herniations and bulges are common in people without symptoms, so an early scan mostly finds lesions unrelated to the pain; up to 85% of patients recover without surgery within 6 weeks whatever the cause.
  • A history of cancer, fever or injection drug use, or a bladder or saddle change, means imaging even when the neurologic exam is normal
  • Night pain that eases on getting up is inflammatory; night pain that no position or analgesic relieves, with a cancer history or weight loss, points to malignancy
    • What it is

    Usually mechanical; a few cases are infection, inflammation, cancer or fracture

    Sort by

    Red flags and the neurologic exam, then how the pain answers rest and movement

    Hands off

    A fragility fracture: Osteoporosis Screening and Treatment; anterior uveitis: The Red Eye; buttock pain from the hip or piriformis: Hip and Thigh Pain and Numbness

    3Urgent risks
    Cauda equina syndromeUrinary retention or incontinence, saddle anesthesia, sciatica on one side or both, lost anal tone and ankle reflexes

    If the bladder or the saddle is involved, choose emergent MRI and surgical decompression.

    Spinal cord compressionUpper motor neuron signs: hyperreflexia (reflexes may be low at first when the onset is acute), an extensor plantar response, a sensory level

    If cancer is known or suspected, choose dexamethasone first, then emergent MRI of the whole spine.

    Spinal epidural abscessFever, focal spinal tenderness and neurologic signs after injection drug use or bacteremia

    If fever comes with a neurologic sign, choose MRI and blood cultures.

    Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysmOlder smoker; sudden back pain with syncope or hypotension; a pulsatile mass

    If the patient is unstable, choose straight to surgery.

    4Differential
    Low back pain, most tempting first
    DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
    Lumbosacral strainAfter lifting; paraspinal tenderness; a symmetric, belt-like acheAcute, settles within weeks; normal neurologic exam, negative straight-leg raise
    Lumbar radiculopathy from a discPain shooting below the knee; positive straight-leg raiseSudden onset; most settle within 6 weeks; imaging (MRI) for a deficit or pain past 6 weeks (the ladder, rung 2)
    Lumbar spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication)Older; buttock and leg pain on walking or standingChronic; eased by sitting or leaning forward (shopping cart, uphill, cycling); pulses normal, unlike vascular claudication
    Ankylosing spondylitis The familySeronegative spondyloarthritis (PAIR: psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, inflammatory bowel disease, reactive arthritis, formerly Reiter syndrome) shares human leukocyte antigen B27 (HLA-B27), enthesitis and anterior uveitis. Ankylosing spondylitis also brings aortic regurgitation (aortitis), stiffens the chest wall (restrictive lung disease), may scar the upper lobes, and thins bone. Its mimic, diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis, affects an older man with flowing ossification over 4 or more vertebrae and normal sacroiliac joints; it is not spondyloarthritis.Man, most often aged 20 to 40; morning stiffness that eases with use; night painInsidious, over 3 months; sacroiliitis on imaging
    Vertebral metastasis RouteProstate cancer reaches the lumbar spine through the vertebral (Batson) venous plexus, often as osteoblastic lesions.Prior cancer (prostate, breast, kidney, thyroid, lung); weight lossWeeks, worsening; night pain that no position or analgesic relieves; MRI with contrast
    Vertebral osteomyelitisInjection drug use, hemodialysis or bacteremia; focal tendernessContinuous pain; fever often absent; ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and CRP (C-reactive protein) high; MRI
    Vertebral compression fractureOlder, osteoporosis or chronic glucocorticoids; a minor fall or liftSudden; point tenderness over one vertebra; radiograph first
    Inflammatory versus mechanical back pain
    FeatureInflammatoryMechanical
    OnsetBy age 40, gradual, over 3 monthsAny age, often sudden after an event
    NightWakes the patient; eases on getting upUsually absent
    Morning stiffnessMarked, eases with useBrief
    Rest and activityWorse with rest, better with exerciseBetter with rest
    5Workup
    Acute low back pain: start on the lowest rung not yet tried
    RungDoMove on when
    1An NSAID or acetaminophen; stay active; a nonbenzodiazepine muscle relaxant second lineStill painful at 4 to 6 weeks, or a new red flag
    2Physical therapy and exerciseRadicular pain past 6 weeks: MRI
    3Epidural glucocorticoid injection, severe or persistent radicular painConservative care fails
    4Surgical referralCauda equina, or an unequivocal disc herniation with a progressive deficit or intractable pain after 6 weeks
    Treatment by cause
    CauseTreatment
    Ankylosing spondylitisAn NSAID and daily exercise, then a TNF (tumor necrosis factor) or IL-17 (interleukin-17) inhibitor

edits.find:
The exam first: gait, joints, bones, calves, reflexes and skin, then the side, the timing and any systemic signs Shared by benign and serious causesGrowing pains, osteoid osteoma and leukemia can all hurt at night, and a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) often eases both growing pains and osteoid osteoma; the side, the exam and systemic signs decide

Hands off

Bone tumors, leukemia, the hot limb and dark urine have their own briefs

3Urgent risks
Respiratory failureAscending weakness with absent reflexes: Guillain-Barré syndrome can paralyze the breathing muscles

If the weakness rises and the reflexes are gone, choose admit; serial spirometry, intubating when the forced vital capacity falls to 20 mL/kg or less (the threshold taught for the exam). Vital capacitya standard clinical reference sets a lower threshold: intubation when the vital capacity falls below 15 mL/kg, checked every 6 to 8 hours

RhabdomyolysisTea-colored urine, a dipstick positive for blood with few red cells, and a CK above 1,000

If the dipstick shows blood with few red cells, choose IV fluids; follow creatinine and potassium.

LeukemiaBone pain with pallor, bruising or fever; the pain can be worse at night and in both legs

If the bones are tender with pallor or bruising, choose CBC with peripheral smear.

Hot limbFever with one-sided point tenderness, warmth or refusal to bear weight: osteomyelitis or septic arthritis

If one leg is tender and the child is febrile, choose ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate), CRP (C-reactive protein) and urgent imaging.

4Differential
Leg pain in a child, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Growing pains (benign nocturnal limb pains of childhood) Growing painsBetween 80% and 90% describe both legs; episodes last minutes to hoursOnset usually 3 to 6 years; calves, thighs, shins or behind the knee, often after active days; late in the day or at night, not during playMonths, with pain-free days: both legs, evening or night, gone by morning; normal exam and gait; no systemic signs
Benign acute childhood myositis (influenza-induced myositis)School-age, more often boys; about 3 days after a flu-like illness, most often influenza B; sudden calf pain, difficulty or refusal to walkDays: calves tender to touch; reflexes preserved; CK high, CRP usually normal Myositis and Guillain-Barré syndromeInfluenza myositis can weaken a child, from mild weakness to quadriparesis, so strength does not separate it from Guillain-Barré syndrome; preserved reflexes do
Guillain-Barré syndromeAfter an infection, influenza among them; symmetric weakness that usually starts in the legs and risesDays to weeks: deep tendon reflexes lost; no calf tenderness; CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) protein may be high with a normal cell count
Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
Dull bone pain, worse at night; refuses to walk; fever, pallor, bruisingTender long bones with pallor or bruising; cytopenias and blasts on the CBC and smear
Bone tumor (osteoid osteoma, osteosarcoma)
One side; persistent or progressive pain; osteoid osteoma hurts at night and NSAIDs relieve itRadiograph: a small lucent nidus (osteoid osteoma), or a destructive lesion with periosteal reaction and a soft-tissue mass (osteosarcoma)
Juvenile dermatomyositisProximal weakness: trouble climbing stairs or rising from a seatWeeks to months: heliotrope rash on the eyelids, Gottron papules on the knuckles; CK high
Arthritis (juvenile idiopathic arthritis, parvovirus B19, rheumatic fever)
Pain in the joint, worse in the morningJoint swelling or reduced range of motion; morning stiffness
Overuse injury (Osgood-Schlatter disease)
Active child after the growth spurt; pain with activityTender tibial tubercle; pain on resisted knee extension

Act now
FindingAction

Temperature instability, lethargy, poor feeding.Obtain cultures and start antibiotics.
Intraventricular hemorrhagePreterm; lethargy, hypotonia, apnea, seizures.Obtain a head ultrasound.

edits.find:
Appendicitis is periumbilical pain that settles at the McBurney point, with anorexia, vomiting and little or no diarrhea: surgical consultation, with imaging before the operation (US first in a child, CT otherwise). Clinical references treat the classic picture as a clinical diagnosis, because delaying surgery for imaging only raises the risk of perforation; the board cards image first.
  • In an adolescent girl, a pregnancy test comes first: ectopic pregnancy is often mistaken for appendicitis.

    • Campylobacter and Yersinia favor the ileocecum, and Yersinia also inflames the mesenteric nodes (mesenteric adenitis); imaging shows ileocecal inflammation with a normal appendix. Campylobacter can begin in the jejunum and then reach the ileum and cecum, so its pain can migrate like appendicitis. In children, appendicitis follows obstruction of the lumen, usually by lymphoid hyperplasia. Bowel movements usually slow or stop in appendicitis; when diarrhea is present, suspect a retrocecal appendix.

Worn enamel or erosive caries in a child who vomits often is acid damage from real, repeated vomiting. It does not mean purging unless there is bingeing, restriction or preoccupation with shape. Onset averages age 5, and it tends to remit by adulthood. The Merck Sharp and Dohme (MSD) Manual describes attacks at varying intervals; the board teaching times them at about the same time each month.

3Urgent risks
Act now

4Differential
Recurrent vomiting: what happens between the episodes
DiagnosisDecides itNext best step
Cyclic vomiting syndromeEntirely well and growing normally between stereotyped, self-limited bouts; often migraine in the child or family.No confirming test: exclude mimics, then treat by cause.
Binges, then compensates; overvalues body shape and weight; parotid swelling and enamel erosion at normal or slightly high weight.Refer for psychiatric assessment.
Bouts like cyclic vomiting with chronic cannabis use; relieved by hot showers or baths (the MSD Manual describes it in adults).Ask about cannabis; urine drug screen.
Inconsistent history, symptoms no one else witnesses; illness caused or fabricated by the caregiver.Notify child protective services.
Gastroesophageal reflux diseaseLow-grade symptoms that persist between bouts; regurgitation and burning substernal pain rather than discrete bursts.Start a trial of acid suppression.
Chronic pancreatitisPoor growth and diarrhea; epigastric tenderness on exam.Order pancreatic imaging and enzyme studies.
Inflammatory bowel diseaseWeight loss and fever; diarrhea and a tender abdomen that persist between bouts.Order blood markers and a colonoscopy.
5Workup
Treatment by cause
CauseTreat
Cyclic vomiting syndromeDuring a bout: IV fluids and an antiemetic; anti-migraine agents such as sumatriptan may help abort it. Avoid its triggers, which are often stress or infection.

edits.find:
A Meckel diverticulum is the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct left partly open, the most common congenital GI anomaly, and most never cause symptoms. Acid from its ectopic gastric mucosa ulcerates the neighboring ileum, which bleeds. The scan images that mucosa rather than the blood, so it works between bleeds. The scan may find the diverticulum in 85 to 97% of bleeding children; a diverticulum with no gastric mucosa does not show.

3Urgent risks
Act now
FindingPoints toAction
Visible bleeding with unstable vital signsA brisk active bleedResuscitate first (intravenous access, fluids, blood); then upper endoscopy for hematemesis or melena, and CT angiography for brisk hematochezia (as for adults); not a Meckel scan.
Infant with bilious vomiting, a distended abdomen and bloody stoolA surgical emergency: upper GI series if stable (The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infant covers it).
4Differential
Bleeding in a well child
DiagnosisDecides itNext best step
Meckel diverticulumToddler, classically under 2 though any age is possible; painless dark red or maroon stool, or occult blood with iron deficiency; soft, nontender abdomen. Often presents by age 2, shorter than 2 inches, 2 feet or less from the ileocecal valve; twice as common in boys.Pertechnetate scan; resect it once it has bled.
Milk protein proctocolitisInfant, well, taking cow's milk protein, with painless blood-streaked stool; resolves by age 1.Remove cow's milk protein from the diet or formula.
Juvenile polypChild with rectal bleeding from a single rectal polyp, which may prolapse.Colonoscopy, which can remove it. Juvenile polyps typically outgrow their blood supply and fall off during or after puberty; removal is needed only for bleeding that will not stop or for intussusception.

edits.find:
The umbilical ring normally closes after the intestines return from their physiologic herniation into the cord; a hernia is a ring that has not closed yet, so skin covers it. Incarceration is very rare, and small hernias usually close on their own. Elective repair of a very large defect may be offered after age 2; the board answer stays repair at about age 5 for a persistent hernia.

3Urgent risks
Act now
FindingPoints toAction
Bowel outside the abdomen at delivery, with or without a membraneGastroschisis or omphaloceleCover it with a sterile, moist dressing, place a nasogastric tube, start IV fluids and antibiotics and keep the infant warm; then surgery. When the bowel will not fit, a silo covers it and is tightened over several days: a staged silo repair.
A known hernia now firm, tender, discolored or irreducible, with vomitingIncarcerated umbilical herniaUrgent surgical repair at any age.
4Differential
A bulge at the umbilicus
FindingDecides itNext best step
Umbilical herniaSkin-covered, soft, reducible, grows with crying; common in normal newborns, more with Down syndrome, hypothyroidism, Beckwith-Wiedemann and Ehlers-Danlos; most common in African-American infants.Observe; repair at about age 5 if it persists.
OmphaloceleMidline, at the umbilical ring; bowel, often liver, in a membrane sac with the cord inserting on it; other major malformations, trisomy 13 or 18, Beckwith-Wiedemann.Repair after birth; order a karyotype and echocardiogram first.
GastroschisisFull-thickness defect, usually right of a normal cord; bare, swollen bowel with no sac; not linked to chromosomal abnormalities.Immediate surgery. Other anomalies are uncommon, but malrotation or intestinal atresia comes with it in about a quarter of infants.

Nodes swell where they drain: a neck node reports on the throat, mouth and scalp, and an arm node on a scratch farther down the limb. An acute hot node is the node itself infected; reactive nodes are many and small; malignant nodes in children are usually painless. In practice: a small node with no flags is rechecked after 10 to 14 days on the board answer; another reference allows up to 4 weeks of observation when there are no other findings.

3Urgent risks
Act now
FindingPoints toAction

Nontender nodes with bruising, pallor, bone pain or hepatosplenomegalyCBC with a smear now (Acute Leukemia in a Child covers the marrow test).
Fever for 5 days or more with a unilateral cervical node, red eyes, rash, strawberry tongue or swollen handsCount the criteria: fever plus 4 of the 5 (Kawasaki Disease covers the workup and treatment).
4Differential

DiagnosisDecides itNext best step

DiagnosisDecides itNext best step

edits.find:
A febrile neonate (28 days or younger) has sepsis until proven otherwise, however well: CBC, blood culture, catheter urine culture and lumbar puncture, then admission on ampicillin plus gentamicin. In practice: the 2021 guideline for well-appearing febrile infants 8 to 60 days old, which the Aquifer case teaches, narrows the 28-day rule above: it taps every infant 21 days or younger, and from 22 to 60 days a well infant may skip the lumbar puncture when inflammatory markers (including procalcitonin, C-reactive protein and absolute neutrophil count) are normal.
  • An ill-appearing infant at any age gets blood and urine cultures and admission, plus a lumbar puncture under 3 months; after the first month the usual drug is IV ceftriaxone.
  • A well child of 3 to 36 months with no source: fully immunized gets only a catheter urine if at risk for a urinary tract infection (UTI); underimmunized adds a CBC and blood culture.

    • When a full history and examination find no focus, a virus is the usual cause; among bacterial sources the urine comes first; the blood, the meninges and the lungs follow. Neonates often do not contain infection locally, and meningeal signs are usually absent under 12 months, so age sets the floor of testing and appearance raises it.

edits.find:
Systemic JIA comes and goes; MAS does not. The fever spikes daily and the rash fades; in MAS the fever is unremitting, the rash constant, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) falls ESRThe ESR depends on fibrinogen; MAS consumes fibrinogen, so the ESR drops even as inflammation peaks.

The uveitis usually gives no symptoms. A slit lamp on a schedule finds it, not a complaint

2Diagnostic criteria
JIA subtypes Age – onset before 16 · Arthritis – 6 weeks or more, no other cause · Systemic – daily fever 2 weeks or more plus rash, nodes, hepatomegaly or splenomegaly, or serositis; boys and girls equally · Polyarticular – 5 or more joints in the first 6 months; girls more · Oligoarticular – 4 or fewer joints in the first 6 months; typically young girls · Enthesitis-related – older boys; HLA-B27
3Urgent risks
LeukemiaLabeled systemic JIA, now pale, petechiae, nodes, hepatosplenomegaly

If two or more cell lines low, choose bone marrow aspiration before treating as JIA or MAS.

MASKnown systemic JIA, now unremitting fever, bleeding, a falling ESR

If ferritin up with platelets, fibrinogen and ESR falling, choose high-dose steroids; high mortality from multiorgan failure. CriteriaIn a febrile child with systemic JIA: ferritin above 684 ng/mL plus any 2 of platelets 181,000/mm³ or less, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) above 48 units/L, triglycerides above 156 mg/dL, fibrinogen 360 mg/dL or less. Built for research; clinicians use them to support the diagnosis.

Septic jointOne hot joint in a child on methotrexate

If fever or one joint out of step with the rest, choose aspirate: septic until the fluid says otherwise.

Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infant

neck rotation and head shape · ear position and sutures · hips and feet

1Script2Criteria3Urgent4Differential5Workup6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Head tilts toward a tight sternocleidomastoid (SCM), chin turns away: congenital muscular torticollis. A firm muscle mass differs from a soft, transilluminating lymphatic malformation.
  • Flat occiput, same-side ear forward: positional plagiocephaly. Ear displaced backward with a suture ridge: suspect lambdoid craniosynostosis and refer for craniofacial evaluation.
  • Stretching and physical therapy, repositioning and awake tummy time; keep supine sleep. Examine hips and feet; a new tilt with neurologic signs needs brain MRI.
What it is

A shortened or fibrotic SCM producing a tilted head usually noticed within the first 3 months

Driver

Intrauterine constraint or neck-muscle injury may contribute

Triggers

Breech positioning or other intrauterine constraint (non-modifiable)

A persistent head-position preference; prematurity increases positional flattening risk

Chain

Restricted neck rotation one-sided positioning pressure-related skull flattening

Insights

The tilt identifies the tight side. The chin points toward the opposite shoulder.

Skull position separates two processes. Forward ear displacement favors pressure-related molding; posterior displacement with a ridge suggests suture fusion.

2Diagnostic criteria
Clinical findings
FindingInterpretation
Fixed tilt with restricted rotation and a firm SCMMuscular torticollis
Anterior ear displacement and same-side forehead prominencePositional deformity is favored
Posterior ear displacement and a suture ridgeSuture fusion is suspected
3Urgent risks
NeurologicNew head tilt in an older child with neurologic findings or chronic-progressive headache

If a central cause is possible, choose obtain brain MRI to evaluate a posterior fossa lesion.

Suture fusionA posteriorly displaced ear on the flat side with a ridge

If craniosynostosis is suspected, choose refer to a craniofacial or neurosurgical team; confirm the suture abnormality.

4Differential
Head tilt, a flat occiput or a neck mass
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Congenital muscular torticollisEarly infant; tight SCM, tilt toward it and chin awayEarly infancy; firm muscle mass that does not transilluminate, with limited neck rotation
Positional plagiocephalyFlat occiput; same-side ear and forehead project forwardA parallelogram shape, without a fused-suture ridge
Lambdoid craniosynostosisFlat occiput with the same-side ear farther backA ridge and trapezoid shape suggest fusion rather than positional molding
Cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation)Soft, compressible posterior-neck massTransilluminates; not a firm contracted SCM
Cervical lymphadenitisTender enlarging node, fever or overlying warmth and rednessInflammation outside the SCM rather than its painless shortening
Posterior fossa tumor Acquired head tilt with neurologic findings in an older childAcquired tilt in an older child; brain MRI, rather than treating it as an infant muscle contracture
5Workup

Keep the calculator and its thresholds together. Current risk assessmentThe 2026 guideline recommends Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease Events (PREVENT) equations for primary prevention in adults ages 30 to 79 without known ASCVD or subclinical atherosclerosis and with LDL 70 to 189 mg/dL. Its risk bands differ: under 3%, 3% to under 5%, 5% to under 10%, and 10% or more. Do not apply the Pooled Cohort cutoffs to a PREVENT result.
Statin-benefit groups
FindingAction
Clinical ASCVD: prior myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke or peripheral artery diseaseUse a high-intensity statin if tolerated; after age 75, a moderate-intensity statin is an option.
LDL ≥ 190 mg/dLUse a high-intensity statin without a risk calculation. Severe LDL elevation is often familial; evaluate for familial hypercholesterolemia and assess relatives.
Diabetes, age 40 to 75Use at least moderate intensity; the board deck favors high intensity when Pooled Cohort risk is 7.5% or more.

Lipid assessment and calculator ages. Periodic risk assessment at ages 40 to 75 includes lipid measurement. The Pooled Cohort Equations are not validated under 40. Screening agesThe US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) standalone adult lipid-screening recommendation is archived; its statin recommendation is risk-based. The board deck also teaches lipid screening from age 20, repeated every 4 to 6 years when normal. Pediatric universal screening is usually during ages 9 to 11, with a second screen during ages 17 to 21. Older USPSTF wording used men 35 or older, women 45 or older at increased risk, and younger adults with risk factors; the conventional interval was about every 5 years. These are legacy screening statements, not the current statin-benefit algorithm.

2Diagnostic criteria

10-year riskCategoryAction

edits.find:
What can precede motor findings? A motor disorder can begin with nonmotor symptoms Nonmotor diseaseAlpha-synuclein pathology extends to olfactory, autonomic and brainstem structures; constipation, reduced smell and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder can precede motor findings

Why combine carbidopa with levodopa? Carbidopa limits peripheral conversion; levodopa reaches the brain Drug pairingLevodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and becomes dopamine. Carbidopa blocks peripheral dopa decarboxylase, reducing nausea and orthostasis while increasing brain delivery; central adverse effects such as agitation and visual hallucinations may still occur Treatment courseLoss of dopamine storage narrows the response window as disease progresses. Delaying levodopa has not been shown to prevent motor complications

What the disease does, by systemSupporting features, not diagnostic alone
MotorSmall handwriting, a quiet voice, reduced facial movement, reduced arm swing and short shuffling steps
AutonomicConstipation, orthostasis, urinary or sexual dysfunction
SleepInsomnia and dream enactment; REM sleep behavior disorder reflects loss of normal REM paralysis
CognitionExecutive and visuospatial impairment may precede memory loss
MoodDepression and anxiety may overlap motor slowing and masked facial expression
PathologyLoss of nigral pigment; Lewy bodies also involve cortex and autonomic structures
Parkinson-plusMultiple system atrophy involves glial alpha-synuclein; progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal degeneration are tauopathiesIn progressive supranuclear palsy, midbrain degeneration can give a hummingbird appearance on MRI
2Diagnostic criteria
Parkinsonism Motor – Bradykinesia plus rigidity or resting tremor · PD – additionally requires no exclusion feature, supportive findings and few or no red flags
TRAPSS
  • Tremor – at rest
  • Rigidity – cogwheel resistance
  • Akinesia/bradykinesia – slow voluntary movement
  • Postural instability – usually late, not required for diagnosis
  • Shuffling gait – short steps
  • Small handwriting – micrographia
3Urgent risks
SwallowingDysphagia can lead to aspiration pneumonia

If swallowing symptoms develop, choose assess swallowing and aspiration risk.

New confusionAcute mental change requires assessment for infection and medication triggers

If confusion or hallucinations newly appear, choose look for a reversible trigger.

DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Parkinson diseaseAsymmetric slowing with rest tremor or rigidityProgressive; clear dopaminergic response; falls usually occur later
Toxic parkinsonismCarbon monoxide exposure or MPTP (an illicit-drug contaminant)Toxin exposure precedes motor disease
Essential tremorBilateral action tremor; head or voice may be involvedAction, rather than rest, brings out the tremor
Drug-induced parkinsonism Dopamine-blocking antipsychotic or antiemetic exposureAfter a drug start or increase; often symmetric; improves after withdrawal
Dementia with Lewy bodies (Lewy body dementia)Fluctuating cognition, formed visual hallucinations and dream enactmentDementia before or within 1 year of motor onset; marked antipsychotic sensitivity
Progressive supranuclear palsyVertical gaze limitation, gait freezing, early fallsEarly falls with vertical gaze palsy; usually poor levodopa response
Multiple system atrophySevere orthostasis or incontinence with ataxia or pyramidal signsEarly autonomic failure; poor dopaminergic response
Corticobasal degenerationAsymmetric motor signs with apraxia, cortical sensory loss or an alien limbCortical dysfunction accompanying parkinsonism; usually little levodopa benefit
Normal pressure hydrocephalusGait impairment, urinary incontinence and cognitive declineAsymmetric rest tremor and rigidity are less typical
Younger patient; liver disease with movement or psychiatric changesCopper-related disease, rather than typical aging-associated PD

can precede motor findings? A motor disorder can begin with nonmotor symptoms WhyNonmotor diseaseAlpha-synuclein pathology extends to olfactory, autonomic and brainstem structures; constipation, reduced smell and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder can precede motor findings

with levodopa? Carbidopa limits peripheral conversion; levodopa reaches the brain MechanismDrug pairingLevodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and becomes dopamine. edits.find:
Neuropathy unfelt trauma at pressure points ulcer contiguous osteomyelitis Fiber typesSmall fibers: pain, burning, autonomic dysfunction (dry skin). Large fibers: sensory loss, which lets injury go unnoticed. It can be present when type 2 diabetes is diagnosed, and diabetes is the most common cause of neuropathic ulcers. Mononeuropathies include cranial nerve III, IV and VI palsies.

Insights

A normal creatinine does not exclude early kidney disease: hyperfiltration may keep it normal

The exam overrules the risk profile: a neuropathic ulcer still needs its perfusion checked PerfusionNeuropathy hides ischemic pain, and calcified vessels raise the ABI, so a normal index makes arterial disease less likely without excluding it.

2Diagnostic criteria
Defining criteria: persistent albuminuria Ratio – UACR 30 mg/g or more · Persistence – 2 of 3 samples over 3 to 6 months · Exclude – exercise, fever, infection, heart failure, hyperglycemia
4Differential
Leg and foot ulcers, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Neuropathic (diabetic) ulcerPainless, plantar over a metatarsal head or heel, callusWarm, dry foot; normal pulses; monofilament not felt
Arterial ulcerPainful toe tips or lateral malleolus, worse elevatedCool, hairless skin; absent pulses; ABI 0.9 or less
Venous stasis ulcerShallow, wet ulcer at the medial malleolusHemosiderin, edema, normal pulses; duplex ultrasound
Charcot arthropathy (neuropathic joint)Weeks of a warm, swollen foot, no ulcer, no feverNeuropathy, normal labs; radiographs or MRI; casting
Pressure ulcerSacrum, heel or trochanter in an immobile patientStaged by depth
Pyoderma gangrenosumDays of rapid, very painful growth; violaceous undermined borderInflammatory bowel disease; biopsy and steroids, never debride
Marjolin ulcer (squamous cell carcinoma in a scar)Over 3 months unhealed in a scar; rolled edgesBiopsy
5Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
"Prevent morbidity"Complications, disabilityScreen for one: the dilated eye exam
"Reduce mortality"DeathSmoking cessation
"Reduce hospitalization"AdmissionsTreat the driver of decompensation
"Most beneficial"Largest effect, any outcomeUsually smoking cessation
Total protein needed, or myeloma suspectedUACR and dipstick miss light chains Light chainsThe dipstick stays negative while the sulfosalicylic acid test is positive; urine electrophoresis shows an M-spike.Protein-to-creatinine ratio or 24-hour urine
Most accurate GFR needed; amputee, cachexiaCreatinine unreliableInulin or iothalamate clearance; cystatin C
Pause point
Screening for nephropathy Offered: a urine dipstick, or reassured by a normal creatinine Hyperfiltration may keep the creatinine normal early → The UACR catches the reversible stage
6Severity
ABI bands
StageABIMeans
NoncompressibleOver 1.4Calcified vessels: use the toe-brachial index
NormalAbout 0.91 to 1.3No arterial disease In practiceIn practice: the American Heart Association reads 1.0 to 1.4 as normal and 0.91 to 0.99 as borderline.
Arterial disease0.9 or lessClaudication range down to 0.4
Critical limb ischemiaUnder 0.4Rest pain, ulcers, gangrene
7Treatment
1

Every patientfrom diagnosis

Glycemic control (A1c goal under 7%) and blood pressure control; a statin from age 40 to 75
2

1st linepersistent albuminuria

ACE inhibitor or ARB (angiotensin receptor blocker), especially with BP over 130/80 In practiceIn practice: some guidance ties the ACE inhibitor or ARB to hypertension; a clinical reference starts it at the first albuminuria whatever the pressure.

Never both together; neither in pregnancy.

3

Addtype 2 diabetes, albuminuria persisting

SGLT2 (sodium-glucose cotransporter 2) inhibitor if the eGFR is 20 or more

It also cuts hyperfiltration.

4

Foot ulcerneuropathic ulcer

Off-load the foot until it heals; inspection at each visit and podiatry
5

Neuropathic painpainful neuropathy

First line: a tricyclic or a gabapentinoid (gabapentin, pregabalin); a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) such as duloxetine is an alternative

Avoid tricyclics over 65 or with heart disease.

6

Referretinopathy moderate or worse

Ophthalmology: macular edema, any proliferative retinopathy, or nonproliferative that is moderate or worse

Proliferative retinopathy: photocoagulation or anti-VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor) therapy.

8Follow-up
Annual care
WhenDo
Type 2: at diagnosis, then yearlyDilated eye exam, UACR with creatinine, monofilament foot exam

If medical treatment fails, choose dialysis (AEIOU).

InfectionNephrotic child with fever and belly pain
Risk is highest in children, in relapse and on long steroid courses
Which antibioticA third-generation cephalosporin such as cefotaxime, pending cultures, as for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in cirrhosis. In nephrotic syndrome: usually Streptococcus pneumoniae.

If fever comes with belly pain or peritoneal signs in a child with ascites, choose diagnostic paracentesis, blood and fluid cultures, then intravenous antibiotics.

If a nephrotic child has these, choose vascular imaging (usually magnetic resonance venography or CT angiography), then long-term anticoagulation unless an invasive intervention is planned.

FindingAction

FindingMeaning

1

NeonateUnder 1 month

IV ampicillin plus cefotaxime, with or without gentamicin; cefotaxime, not ceftriaxone, because ceftriaxone raises bilirubin. Ampicillin covers Listeria; cefotaxime enters the central nervous system better than gentamicin.

2

Child or adultOver 1 month

IV vancomycin plus ceftriaxone: ceftriaxone covers meningococcus and other gram-negatives; vancomycin is added for cephalosporin-resistant pneumococcus. In practice: once the organism and its susceptibilities are known, therapy narrows and vancomycin may stop.

3

Listeria riskOver 50, pregnancy or immunocompromise

Add IV ampicillin for Listeria.

AdjunctSuspected Hib or pneumococcal meningitis after 6 weeks of age

IV dexamethasone just before or with the first antibiotic dose, every 6 hours for 4 days, to cut hearing loss. In adults it is best established for pneumococcal meningitis; high-dose steroids worsen meningococcal shock without meningitis.

HSV possibleEncephalitis signs or lymphocytes with red cells

Add IV acyclovir until HSV is ruled out.

6

Shunt or neurosurgeryVentricular shunt or recent neurosurgery

Vancomycin plus an antipseudomonal beta-lactam such as cefepime.

WhenDo

Schizophrenia: genes explain about 80% of the risk in twin and family studies Schizophrenia, proposed mechanismProposed: excess mesolimbic dopamine is thought to contribute to positive symptoms; lower mesocortical dopamine may be involved in negative and cognitive symptoms

Triggers

Family history non-modifiable Cannabis risk6 times the risk in one study

A marked stressor, or onset during pregnancy or PostpartumPostpartum brief psychotic disorder raises the risk of suicide and infanticide. (brief psychotic disorder)

Chain

Schizophrenia: prodrome active psychosis, 1 month or more (less if treated) residual; 6 months in all CourseSchizophreniform may evolve into schizophrenia, bipolar or schizoaffective disorder

Insights

Symptoms outlast a window re-time the whole illness

Criterion A with a mood episode psychosis 2 weeks or more without one mood most of the illness schizoaffective

Course and specifiersdetail behind the chain
Brief psychotic1 day to under 1 month, then full return to baseline; specifiers: with marked stressor; with postpartum onset
Schizophrenia6 months or more, with functional decline; Age at onsetOnset runs from the late teens to the mid-30s, so a teen can have it; childhood onset is rare and has a poorer prognosis.
2Diagnostic criteria
Defining criteria: schizophrenia Criterion A, symptoms – 2 or more of delusions, hallucinations, In a vignetteDisorganized speech: nonsensical or unrelated answers. Catatonia may show mutism, purposeless movement, fixed postures or staring., disorganized or catatonic behavior, negative symptoms, such as alogia (little speech): In a vignetteAvolition: began to wear the same clothes for several days in a row; poorly groomedNegative symptoms: Social withdrawal, poor eye contact, neglected hygiene, lost motivation, flat affect, little speech, no pleasure. They count toward Criterion A.Disorganized behavior: sending e-mails to his friends, though he had not been connected to the internet for 3 months · Criterion A, core – at least 1 is delusions, hallucinations or disorganized speech · Duration – 6 months or more in all, with at least 1 month of active symptoms (less if treated) · Decline – work or relationships fall since onset · Cause – not a substance, medication or medical condition; schizoaffective and psychotic mood disorders excluded
3Urgent risks
DangerLikely harm to self or others, or cannot meet basic needs
American Psychiatric Association positionA mental disorder; hospital care can help; the patient is unable or unwilling to consent; the least restrictive option. Commitment law varies by state.

If harm is likely or basic needs go unmet, choose hospitalization first, whatever the duration; involuntarily only when the criteria and state law allow.

MedicalPsychosis with disturbed attention and awareness that develops over hours to days and fluctuates

If it occurs only during a delirium, choose the delirium workup, not a psychotic disorder.

4Differential
Look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
SchizophreniaCriterion A with functional decline6 months or more, at least 1 month active
Delusional disorder1 or more delusions, often Delusion themesThemes: persecutory (being harmed), referential (cues aimed at the self), grandiose, erotomanic (another person is in love with the patient), jealous (a partner is unfaithful; the person typically searches for evidence), somatic, nihilistic (the self or world does not exist or is ending). (eg, somatic: sure of a parasite infestation); hallucinations, if any, not prominent and tied to the delusion; apart from the delusion, functioning not markedly impaired1 month or more; no second Criterion A symptom
Brief psychotic disorder1 or more core symptoms, often after a stressor1 day to under 1 month; full return to baseline
Schizophreniform disorderCriterion A1 to under 6 months; functional decline not required
Schizoaffective disorderCriterion A with major mood episodes at the same timePsychosis 2 weeks or more without a mood episode; mood most of the illness
Bipolar type includes a manic episode; depressive type, only major depressive episodes
Delusions with euphoric mood and less sleepMania 1 week or more (any length if hospitalized); psychosis only inside mood episodes
(medication-induced psychotic disorder, when a medication is the cause)Delusions or hallucinations tied to a drugDuring or soon after intoxication or withdrawal, or after a medication; lasting about 1 month after stopping suggests an independent disorder
Distress after a stressorWithin 3 months of the stressor; psychosis would be atypical
Symptoms after an eventMore than 1 month; trauma that threatens death or injury; intrusions and avoidance
The pictureIntrusive re-experiencing with hyperarousal, dissociation and avoidance, for up to 1 month. Hallucinations after the stressor point to brief psychotic disorder instead.3 days to 1 month after a trauma
(psychotic depression)Psychosis with major depressive episodesPsychosis only inside the depressive episodes
Psychosis from a metabolic or thyroid illness, such as hypothyroidismAbnormal chemistry, glucose or TSH, with psychosis timed to it

No cause found: time the psychosis, then check it against mood episodes.

Typically levator ani (pelvic floor) dysfunction involuntary contraction when a finger is inserted In practice:Merck Manual notes that, because symptoms typically come from levator ani dysfunction, the term levator ani syndrome is increasingly used in place of vaginismus. On the exam, the answer is vaginismus or GPPPD; levator syndrome in a rectal pain stem is a different disorder, episodic rectal pain from levator ani spasm.

Triggers

History of abuse non-modifiable, anxiety disorders, relationship conflict, cultural taboos; not present in every patient

Can also follow a vulvar infection such as candidiasis, a gynecologic problem such as endometriosis, or pregnancy

Chain

Anticipated pain fear pelvic floor tightens on the attempt more pain and failed penetration more fear, and avoidance may follow

Examination typically normal apart from a tight pelvic floor

Insights

Normal tissue and swab a pelvic floor that contracts on one finger GPPPD when about 6 months with distress; an infection, lesion or atrophy on examination treat that cause first

Anxiety only about penetration: not GAD (generalized anxiety disorder); pain without preoccupation: not somatic symptom disorder

Criteria and course, part by partdetail behind the chain
Criterion APersistent or recurrent trouble with one or more of four: penetration during intercourse; marked vulvovaginal or pelvic pain with intercourse or attempts; marked fear or anxiety about that pain before, during or after penetration; marked tensing of the pelvic floor on the attempt
DurationAbout 6 months or longer: DSM-5 says approximately 6 months, and Merck Manual gives the DSM-5-TR (fifth edition, text revision) version as at least 6 months
ExclusionsNot better explained by a nonsexual mental disorder, severe relationship distress such as partner violence, or other major stressors; not due to a substance, a medication or another medical condition
Risk factorsAbuse, anxiety disorders, relationship conflict, cultural taboos; some patients have none
SecondaryAfter a vulvar infection such as candidiasis, a gynecologic problem such as endometriosis, or pregnancy
2Diagnostic criteria
Defining criteria: genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder Symptoms – one or more of penetration difficulty, marked pain with attempts, marked fear of that pain, or marked pelvic floor tightening on the attempt · Duration – Guideline detailDSM-5 says approximately 6 months; Merck Manual Professional gives the DSM-5-TR version as at least 6 months with significant distress. or longer · Distress – clinically significant · Exclusions – no nonsexual mental disorder, severe relationship distress such as partner violence, or major stressor explains it better; no substance, medication or medical cause
3Urgent risks
SafetyPartner violence: ask about it directly, in private

If partner violence is disclosed or suspected, choose a check of her immediate risk and a safety plan made with her.

4Differential
Look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Vulvodynia Exam detailNBME's explanation describes the spontaneous form: vulvar, not vaginal, pain that penetration does not typically provoke. The provoked form, localized to the vestibule (provoked vestibulodynia), does hurt on entry with a tampon or intercourse. Either way, the cotton swab finds the tender spot; in GPPPD the vestibule is not tender to light touch and the pelvic floor contracts. Trauma, then intrusive memories or nightmares; may avoid remindersMore than 1 month of symptoms; intrusions and avoidance tied to the trauma, not only to penetration
Little interest or arousal; no pain6 months; at least 3 of 6 symptoms; distress
Genitourinary syndrome of menopausePostmenopausal burning and drynessMay show pale, dry tissue (may look normal in early menopause)

CluePoints toNext best step
Normal vulva; painless swab; pelvic floor contracts on one fingerGPPPDPelvic floor physical therapy with CBT

1. DeliriumSudden, hours to days; lasts days to weeks, sometimes longer; fluctuates, worse at night
    HoursDaysWeeksMonthsYears→

    AttentionGreatly impaired

    OrientationVaries; time most often affected

    PsychosisVisual hallucinations common; delusions can occur

  2. Major neurocognitive disorder (dementia)Slow, uncertain start; progressive, stable day to day
    HoursDaysWeeksMonthsYears→

    AttentionSpared until severe

    OrientationImpaired

    PsychosisHallucinations rare until late, except in Lewy body dementia

  3. Primary psychosisUsually slow, with a prodrome; chronic, with exacerbations
    HoursDaysWeeksMonthsYears→

    AttentionAlmost never impaired; altered consciousness suggests a medical cause

    OrientationDisorientation suggests a medical cause

    PsychosisHallucinations mainly auditory

Dementia is a leading risk factor: judge the change against the baseline from someone who knows the patient.

3Urgent risks
WithdrawalDelirium tremens: confusion, fleeting hallucinations, tremor, sweating, fever and a fast pulse, usually 48 to 96 hours after the last drink
It can be fatal: treat it promptly

If alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal is the cause, choose an intravenous (IV) benzodiazepine; in alcohol withdrawal, no haloperidol at first.

NutritionalHeavy drinking or malnutrition, with confusion, nystagmus or eye-movement palsy, and an unsteady gait
Glucose given first can precipitate it

If Wernicke encephalopathy (from thiamine deficiency) is possible, choose IV thiamine before any glucose.

DangerAgitation that puts the patient or others at risk
Restraint only to prevent harm

If it threatens safety despite nonpharmacologic care and withdrawal is excluded, choose a low-dose antipsychotic, with a baseline electrocardiogram (ECG) for the QTc (the QT, or Q wave to T wave, interval corrected for heart rate), especially with haloperidol.

NeurologicNew focal sign or head trauma

If a subdural bleed or stroke is possible, choose noncontrast CT (computed tomography) of the head, the first-line scan.

InfectionSuspected bacterial meningitis

If lumbar puncture must wait for imaging, choose blood cultures, then antibiotics and a glucocorticoid before the scan.

Reversethe opioid overdose triad

Naloxone, with bag-mask breaths until it works

The reversal agent can wear off before the opioid, so observe; it can precipitate withdrawal. Given quickly, it rarely leaves a need for intubation.

2

1st lineagitation from PCP, cocaine or amphetamine

A benzodiazepine, intravenous or intramuscular

Lowers central sympathetic outflow. For cocaine, nitrates or an alpha-blocker if chest pain or hypertension persists after this first drug. Guideline detailLorazepam 2 to 4 mg or diazepam 5 to 10 mg, intravenous or intramuscular

1st linemoderate to severe alcohol withdrawal

Guideline detailCIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, revised) or SAWS (Short Alcohol Withdrawal Scale) scores set the as-needed doses Long-acting chlordiazepoxide or diazepam; in the hospital, intravenous lorazepam; with cirrhosis or alcoholic hepatitis, lorazepam or oxazepam, whose glucuronidation liver disease spares. Buprenorphine or methadone

Distressing, not dangerous, after a spontaneous stop. Start buprenorphine only once withdrawal signs are clear: a partial agonist given while a full agonist is still on board displaces it and precipitates withdrawal. Guideline detailSublingual buprenorphine 4 to 12 mg to start, an alternative to methadone

Clonidine

Can ease autonomic signs, such as blood pressure, in opioid withdrawal; in alcohol withdrawal only as an adjunct to a benzodiazepine.

6

Flumazenil in a long-term user; urinary acidification for PCP; beta-blockers in cocaine toxicity

Guideline detailFlumazenil is best kept for respiratory depression during a procedure.

Confused, sweating and tachycardic days after the last drink Offered as alcoholic hallucinosis Disorientation with autonomic instability; hallucinosis keeps a clear sensorium → Delirium tremens: a benzodiazepine, thiamine before glucose
Agitated patient, urine screen pending Offered: waiting on the screen before treating The toxidrome is read at the bedside; routine screens often miss synthetic cathinones → Treat the toxidrome now
7Treatment
1

Reversethe opioid overdose triad

Naloxone, with bag-mask breaths until it works

The reversal agent can wear off before the opioid, so observe; it can precipitate withdrawal. Given quickly, it rarely leaves a need for intubation.

2

1st lineagitation from PCP, cocaine or amphetamine

A benzodiazepine, intravenous or intramuscular

. For cocaine, nitrates or an alpha-blocker if chest pain or hypertension persists after this first drug. PCP dosingGuideline detailLorazepam 2 to 4 mg or diazepam 5 to 10 mg, intravenous or intramuscular

3

1st linemoderate to severe alcohol withdrawal

A benzodiazepine, dosed by withdrawal scale score

Guideline detailCIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, revised) or SAWS (Short Alcohol Withdrawal Scale) scores set the as-needed doses Long-acting chlordiazepoxide or diazepam; in the hospital, intravenous lorazepam; with cirrhosis or alcoholic hepatitis, lorazepam or oxazepam, whose glucuronidation liver disease spares. Also for seizures (not routine phenytoin) and, intravenously and promptly, delirium tremens; Why notAntipsychotics may lower the seizure threshold, already low in alcohol withdrawal.. With intravenous fluids, thiamine before glucose. Thiamine doseGuideline detail100 mg intravenously, before any glucose

4

1st lineopioid withdrawal

Buprenorphine or methadone

, not dangerous, after a spontaneous stop. Start buprenorphine only once withdrawal signs are clear: a partial agonist given while a full agonist is still on board displaces it and precipitates withdrawal. DoseGuideline detailSublingual buprenorphine 4 to 12 mg to start, an alternative to methadone

5

Adjunctautonomic signs

Clonidine

Can ease autonomic signs, such as blood pressure, in opioid withdrawal; in alcohol withdrawal only as an adjunct to a benzodiazepine.

6

Avoidtempting but wrong

Flumazenil in a long-term user; urinary acidification for PCP; beta-blockers in cocaine toxicity

Guideline detailFlumazenil is best kept for respiratory depression during a procedure.

Serotonin transporter blocked more serotonin in the synapse longer postsynaptic stimulation Serotonin receptorsType 1 receptors carry the antidepressant and anti-anxiety effect; type 2 receptors bring anxiety, insomnia and sexual dysfunction; type 3 receptors bring nausea and headache. Dopamine and norepinephrine are barely touched.

Few anticholinergic or cardiac conduction effects wide safety margin; isolated overdose is usually well tolerated, except with citalopram

Uses

Depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, panic, generalized and social anxiety, premenstrual dysphoric disorder; fluoxetine for bulimia nervosa Other usesSSRIs also treat premature ejaculation and menopausal hot flashes (paroxetine, citalopram).

Adverse effects

Monoamine oxidase (MAO) A and B blocked, irreversibly less breakdown of serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine The two enzymesMAO‑A breaks down serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine. MAO‑B breaks down dopamine. Phenelzine, tranylcypromine and isocarboxazid block both; selegiline at low doses and rasagiline block MAO‑B selectively.

Gut MAO‑A blocked dietary tyramine enters the circulation norepinephrine pushed out of nerve endings hypertensive crisis

Irreversible block new enzyme must be made diet limits and washout outlast the last dose (timeline below)

Selegiline: MAO‑B only at low doses gut MAO‑A spared at the low-dose patch

Uses

Treatment-resistant depression, atypical depression, anxiety; not first line Why MAOIs are reservedKept for severe, treatment-resistant depression because of the hypertensive crisis and their lethality in overdose. Tranylcypromine often works after several failed antidepressant trials.

Atypical features (mood brightens with good news, more sleep and appetite, leaden paralysis): other first-line drugs first, an MAOI if they fail

Selegiline: also Parkinson disease, as an MAO‑B inhibitor added when levodopa starts to wear off; may worsen levodopa adverse effects

Adverse effects

Hypertensive crisis and serotonin syndrome: the two blocks below

Lethal in overdose

Common: erectile dysfunction, insomnia and anxiety (central nervous system stimulation), dizziness, nausea, pedal edema, weight gain Dose timingDoses go in the morning and early afternoon to avoid overstimulation. Erectile dysfunction is least common with tranylcypromine.

Withdrawal after an abrupt stop: vivid nightmares, agitation, psychosis, seizures; timing below

Orthostatic (postural) hypotension

Tyramine crisisSevere hypertension, occipital headache, blurry vision and sweating within minutes of aged cheese, aged meats, wine or malted beer, or a decongestant such as pseudoephedrine

If a hypertensive crisis follows tyramine on an MAOI, choose phentolamine, an alpha blocker that dilates vessels. Other antidotes offeredCyproheptadine treats serotonin syndrome. Physostigmine treats severe anticholinergic toxicity, with hot, dry skin.

Headache, a fast or slow pulse, or chest pain on an MAOI may mean a rise in blood pressure; intracranial bleeding has been reported

Serotonin syndromeFever, mental status changes, autonomic instability, hyperreflexia and clonus after a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI), tricyclic, meperidine, tramadol, dextromethorphan, linezolid or St. John's wort

If serotonin syndrome appears, choose stopping every serotonergic drug.

Combined withResultRule

Meperidine, tramadol, dextromethorphanSerotonin syndromeAvoid
Linezolid, a weak MAOISerotonin syndromeAvoid
Pseudoephedrine, other sympathomimeticsHypertensive crisisAvoid

, not acute mania Lamotrigine"Relapsigine": lamotrigine prevents relapse.

Oxcarbazepine: matches carbamazepine for mood with fewer adverse effects, including less rash and less liver toxicity

Topiramate: prevents migraine and treats binge eating disorder; it has shown no benefit in bipolar disorder

Lithium: tremor, nystagmus, polyuria and thirst, hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, or arginine vasopressin resistance (nephrogenic) Nephrogenic diabetes insipidusLithium builds up in collecting duct cells and blocks the action of antidiuretic hormone (ADH), so free water is lost.

Valproate: GI upset (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea), weight gain, sedation, tremor, ataxia, hair loss ValproateHair loss in 5% to 10%. Hyperandrogenism in women; it may raise the risk of polycystic ovary syndrome.

Valproate, rare but serious: hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, hyperammonemic encephalopathy, thrombocytopenia HyperammonemiaA valproate metabolite, propionic acid, stops the urea cycle clearing ammonia; liver failure or a urea cycle disorder is a reason not to use it.

Carbamazepine: sleepiness, nausea, diarrhea, rash; double vision (diplopia), ataxia CarbamazepineVitamin D deficiency may occur: the induced enzyme breaks vitamin D down.

Carbamazepine, serious: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, low sodium, liver toxicity

Oxcarbazepine: fatigue, dizziness, somnolence, double vision; hyponatremia OxcarbazepineAbout 25% to 30% of patients with a carbamazepine hypersensitivity reaction react to oxcarbazepine too (label).

Topiramate: weight loss, kidney stones, sedation, cognitive slowing, speech dysfunction; myopia with acute angle-closure glaucoma; metabolic acidosis Topiramate labelThe acidosis is hyperchloremic, with a normal anion gap. Decreased sweating (oligohidrosis) is reported.

Other

Pregnancy, valproate: neural tube defects and other major malformations Valproate in pregnancyAlso oral clefts, heart and urogenital malformations; in childhood, cognitive deficits, autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder.

Pregnancy, carbamazepine: neural tube, heart and craniofacial defects

Pregnancy, lithium: Ebstein anomaly and other heart defects

Pregnancy, topiramate: cleft lip or palate; lamotrigine: relatively safe PregnancyUse in the first trimester may raise the risk of oral clefts slightly. Topiramate can also leave the baby small for gestational age.

Rash on lamotrigineA benign rash and early SJS or TEN cannot be told apart

Risk is higher in children, with valproate, or with a fast titration

If a rash of any kind appears on lamotrigine, choose stopping lamotrigine and switching to another agent.

DRESS (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms)A polymorphic rash, typically with liver or other organ involvement, 2 to 8 weeks into carbamazepine or lamotrigine

Eosinophilia is often present (lamotrigine label) Lamotrigine skinSJS is the most serious skin reaction on lamotrigine.

If DRESS appears, choose stopping the drug.

Valproate pancreatitisEpigastric pain and vomiting with a raised lipase; idiosyncratic, so dose and years on the drug do not rule it out

In most cases it resolves after the cause is removed

If acute pancreatitis appears on valproate, choose stopping valproate.

Confusion on valproateDrowsiness or confusion on valproate: a metabolite blocks the urea cycle

Once the diagnosis is confirmed: stop valproate and look for an underlying urea cycle disorder

If confusion develops on valproate, choose checking plasma ammonia.

Valproate toxicity with GI symptomsVomiting, diarrhea and confusion on valproate

Carbamazepine blood dyscrasiaAgranulocytosis or aplastic anemia, typically in the first 3 to 4 months

Clozapine also causes agranulocytosis

If a blood dyscrasia appears on carbamazepine, choose stopping carbamazepine; some of these recover after the stop.

Carbamazepine in Asian ancestryAn allele typical of Asian ancestry carries the SJS and TEN risk on carbamazepine

If carbamazepine is planned in a patient of Asian ancestry, choose HLA-B*1502 testing first, and avoiding the drug if the allele is present.

Low sodium on carbamazepine or oxcarbazepineConfusion with a low sodium: syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH), dose-dependent, on carbamazepine; hyponatremia on oxcarbazepine

If the hyponatremia is symptomatic, choose considering a stop of carbamazepine; with oxcarbazepine, some patients need a lower dose, a stop or fluid limits.

Carbamazepine overdoseSodium channel block can widen the QRS Carbamazepine overdoseAnticholinergic effects (hyperthermia, flushed skin, dilated pupils), tachycardia and hypotension. Care is mainly supportive.

Levels are repeated until they fall: the peak can take days

If the QRS is wide or the rhythm is abnormal, choose sodium bicarbonate; continuous cardiac monitoring may be needed.

Valproate overdoseLethargy; anion gap metabolic acidosis, hypernatremia, hypocalcemia, high ammonia Valproate overdoseGlucose, acetaminophen and salicylate levels, and an electrocardiogram; in severe cases sodium, bicarbonate, calcium, ammonia, platelets and liver tests.

Hemodialysis may remove much of the drug in overdose

If a valproate overdose is suspected, choose valproate levels every 2 to 3 hours, since a delayed-release tablet can peak late.

Clorazepate ⚠︎ pharm document line; no board source found yet

Mechanism

Binds its own site on the gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) type A receptor chloride channel opens more often sedation, anxiolysis, seizure control Versus barbituratesBenzodiazepines raise how often the channel opens ("frenzodiazepines"). Barbiturates bind a different site, carry more risk of respiratory depression and coma, and are not reversed by flumazenil.

Long use GABA-A receptors downregulate tolerance withdrawal after an abrupt stop

Agents cleared by glucuronidation alone skip the oxidative liver step safer in liver disease and old age MnemonicLOT may help recall them: lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam, safe in liver disease.

Uses

Anxiety, panic: a short-term bridge until a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) works

Insomnia: not first line (dependence)

Alcohol withdrawal: long-acting agents, or lorazepam with liver disease

Catatonia (first line)

Status epilepticus, procedural sedation, acute agitation

Adverse effects

Sedation, ataxia, anterograde amnesia; older adults: falls, confusion

Rebound anxiety between doses of a short-acting agent Interdose symptomsThe Xanax label reports early-morning anxiety and anxiety between doses in panic disorder on maintenance doses.

Physiologic dependence on prescribed use is not a use disorder

Addiction: higher with short-acting agents MnemonicATOM may help recall the more addictive group: alprazolam, triazolam, oxazepam, midazolam (alprazolam and oxazepam are intermediate in some tables).

Withdrawal after an abrupt stop; timing below

Disinhibition in an adolescent raises acute suicide risk

Respiratory depressionStupor, slow breathing, low blood pressure with an opioid or alcohol; alone, near-normal vital signs and pupils

Flumazenil needs caution: in a long-term user it can set off withdrawal and seizures

If breathing slows or blood pressure falls, choose airway, breathing and circulation support; naloxone if an opioid may be involved.

Withdrawal seizuresTremor, anxiety, then a seizure within 1 to 2 days of stopping a short-acting agent such as alprazolam

If a daily user must come off a benzodiazepine, choose a slow taper, ideally of a longer-acting agent.

If agitation follows a benzodiazepine dose, choose tapering and stopping it; a higher dose only worsens it.

edits.find:
Guanfacine Intuniv, clonidine: nonstimulant alpha-2 agonists Guanfacine formsExtended-release guanfacine is not swapped milligram for milligram with the immediate-release tablet; the two are absorbed differently.

Mechanism

Methylphenidate: dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake blocked more of both at the synapse

Amphetamines: catecholamines displaced from storage vesicles released into the synapse

Lisdexamfetamine: activated in the gut usable with a drug-misuse history

Atomoxetine: norepinephrine transporter blocked no action on the nucleus accumbens no addiction risk

Guanfacine, clonidine: alpha-2 agonists less presynaptic norepinephrine release hypotension, bradycardia, sleepiness

Uses

ADHD: by age as in the Key point Preschool childrenBehavioral therapy comes first; medication may be considered if the response is inadequate or symptoms are moderate to severe.

Atomoxetine when a stimulant is ruled out, as with a high risk of misuse or diversion; alpha-2 agonists when stimulants fail, in children and teens Alpha-2 agonists in ADHDGuanfacine works better than clonidine for childhood ADHD. Both are less effective than stimulants and have limited data in adults.

Lisdexamfetamine: also binge eating disorder

Narcolepsy: methylphenidate or an amphetamine, second line after modafinil

Methylphenidate: also used in severe depression when life expectancy is short

Clonidine, guanfacine: also tics

Adverse effects

Stimulants: appetite suppression (the dose can be taken after a meal), insomnia, higher HR and BP Other effectsHeadache and stomachache are also common. On average, a stimulant raises the heart rate by 5-10 beats/min and systolic BP by 4-6 mm Hg.

Growth in height slows over 2 years of use; adult height may be lower

Tics can emerge on a stimulant; they do not rule one out

New psychotic or manic symptoms are a label warning; in diagnosed bipolar disorder, a small risk of switching to mania Stimulant labelsSudden death is reported with structural heart disease. Peripheral vasculopathy, including Raynaud phenomenon: watch the fingers and toes.

Misuse and diversion: high abuse potential; family members prescribed stimulants are one route to misuse Prescribed useOn a prescribed, supervised stimulant, tolerance and withdrawal alone do not make a stimulant use disorder.

Atomoxetine: nausea, sedation, irritability; rare liver injury; suicidal ideation in children and teens (boxed warning) Atomoxetine contraindicationsContraindicated with narrow-angle glaucoma, a present or past pheochromocytoma, or severe heart or vessel disease that a rise in BP or HR would worsen.

Alpha-2 agonists: sleepiness, low BP, slow pulse, fainting on standing (orthostatic syncope); rebound hypertension after an abrupt stop Added sedationOther central nervous system depressants add to the sleepiness.

Mania on a stimulantAn episodic course fits bipolar disorder better than chronic ADHD

Dilated pupils (mydriasis) and a fast pulse point to stimulant intoxication instead

If a manic episode begins on a stimulant, choose tapering or stopping the stimulant and treating the mania first.

Atomoxetine liver injuryItching, dark urine, jaundice or right upper quadrant tenderness on atomoxetine, with raised liver enzymes

If jaundice or laboratory evidence of liver injury appears, choose stopping atomoxetine and never restarting it.

Alpha-2 reboundHeadache, agitation, tremor, then a sharp rise in BP and pulse after guanfacine or clonidine is stopped suddenly or doses are missed ReboundHypertensive encephalopathy has followed an abrupt stop.

Doses often missed favor another drug

If guanfacine or clonidine is to be stopped, choose a slow taper, with BP and HR checked at each step.

Interactions, by result
Combined withResultRule
Monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI), linezolid included, with a stimulant or atomoxetineWith a stimulant, hypertensive crisis; with atomoxetine, fever, rigidity, unstable vital signs Contraindicated during the MAOI and through its washout
Fluoxetine or paroxetine, with atomoxetineAtomoxetine exposure up 6- to 8-fold (liver enzyme cytochrome P450 2D6 blocked)Raise the atomoxetine dose more slowly (timeline below)
Monitoring
WhenCheckWhy
Before a stimulantCardiac history and exam; BP, HR, height, weightSudden death with structural heart disease; a baseline to compare against
Throughout stimulant useBP and HR, height and weight on growth charts, sleep, appetite, tics

edits.find:
Nicotine replacement: NicoDerm CQ (patch), gum or lozenge Nicorette for cravings; the patch keeps a steady level Nicotine replacementIn practice: combined nicotine forms work about as well as varenicline.

Mechanism

Naltrexone: mu receptor blocked opioid euphoria blocked; less craving and fewer heavy drinking days Naloxone or naltrexoneNaloxone treats toxicity; naltrexone prevents relapse.

Acamprosate: glutamate modulated less craving once abstinent

Disulfiram: acetaldehyde dehydrogenase blocked acetaldehyde builds after a drink Disulfiram reactionThink of the reaction as a really bad hangover: acetaldehyde causes hangover symptoms.

Buprenorphine: high affinity, low efficacy a ceiling on respiratory depression

Naloxone in the combination: inactive under the tongue; injected, it precipitates withdrawal deters misuse

Methadone: long half-life steady receptor activation no withdrawal, less craving Methadone accumulationIt can build up faster than it is cleared.

Varenicline: nicotinic partial agonist less withdrawal and craving Varenicline receptorThe alpha-4 beta-2 nicotinic receptor (label). It also partly blocks the effects of nicotine. Nicotine withdrawal brings irritability, anxiety, restlessness and poor concentration.

Uses

Alcohol use disorder: naltrexone or acamprosate first line, acamprosate preferred with liver disease or opioid use; disulfiram second line; alongside psychosocial treatment

Opioid use disorder: buprenorphine or methadone maintenance first line, often long term; long-acting naltrexone after withdrawal, for mild disorder Opioid maintenanceWhen maintenance is going well, continue it; in a highly motivated patient a slow taper may be tried, with close watch for relapse.

Opioid use disorder in pregnancy: methadone or buprenorphine PregnancyBetter maternal and newborn outcomes than abstinence.

Quitting smoking: varenicline, nicotine replacement and bupropion are all first line

Adverse effects

Naltrexone: hepatotoxicity; precipitated withdrawal with opioids on board

Acamprosate: diarrhea; kidney-cleared, so avoid with significant impairment Acamprosate labelIn practice: the label contraindicates it at a creatinine clearance of 30 mL/min or less.

Disulfiram: reaction with any alcohol (see the disulfiram reaction row below); not in pregnancy or cardiac decompensation Disulfiram labelHepatitis, sometimes fatal, may develop even after months; optic and peripheral neuritis may occur; contraindicated with psychosis or severe myocardial disease. Never given to an intoxicated patient or without the patient knowing.

What actually decides the question, and how else they can ask it. Every entry names the fork, tables the mimics, and banks the variants.

How to Use This

The clinical content is downstream of the method. Read this section once, then let the briefs reinforce it.

Method guide – the three habits, question verbs & the trap speciestap to expand

The three habits

  1. The assassin scan. For each answer choice, find the sentence in the stem that makes it impossible. When every option but one has an assassin, the question is finished – no forward reasoning required. A stem's "normal" findings are eliminations, not filler.
  2. The switch rule. Change an answer only when rereading reveals a misread fact – never when it reveals a new possibility. A detail that is merely compatible with another diagnosis is flavor. Incompatibility, not plausibility.
  3. Store the discriminator, not the outcome. Learn "limping child → score Kocher," never "limping child → aspirate." Rules stored as outcomes fire on the benign mirror-twin stem and get you twice.

Read the verb before the choices

  1. "Most likely diagnosis" → the diagnosis that explains all findings, not the most findings.
  2. "Most sensitive / screening" → lowest detection threshold. "Most accurate / definitive / confirms" → tissue, or the gold-standard test.
  3. "Next step in management" → the next rung on the ladder. "Next step in diagnosis" → the test whose result changes what you do tonight.
  4. "Most beneficial / reduces mortality" → match the intervention's time-to-benefit to the outcome's time horizon. Lipids = years. BP, volume, GDMT = weeks to months.
  5. "Underlying cause" → the trunk of the causal tree, not a branch.
The ten trap species
SpeciesHow it worksAntidote
Salient decoyA vivid, concrete detail – occupation, travel, family history – that is compatible with the right answer but suggests a wrong one. Camping in Georgia → Lyme, when the answer is rheumatic fever.Ask what job the detail is doing. If it's making you nervous rather than deciding anything, it's bait.
Treat-the-numberAn abnormal lab planted so you medicate the value instead of the outcome. Low HDL → niacin. High A1c → metformin. High Hct → phlebotomy.Ask which intervention changes the outcome named in the question.
Trump-card inversionA risk calculator offered when a categorical indication already decides it. 10-year risk 4.9% in a diabetic – diabetes already earned the statin.Check trump cards before calculators: prior event, LDL ≥190, diabetes 40–75.
True-fact-wrong-slotA real association placed where the timeline or findings forbid it. Post-URI in a 12-month history. Fibroids causing postmenopausal bleeding.Verify the interval and the physiologic state before you use the association.
Mirror twinThe benign version of a stem you just learned the dangerous version of. Transient synovitis right after septic arthritis.Store the scoring rule, not the action.
Sequencing trapA correct action offered one step out of order. MRI before conservative therapy. Antibiotics before aspiration. Imaging before airway.Name the ladder out loud before choosing a rung.
Uniform-answer doubtAn "all yes" or "no further testing" option rejected because it feels too easy. HIV vaccine grid – the answer really was yes to all four.Reject it only with a named disqualifying criterion you can say out loud.
Test-overrides-findingsA normal or discordant test offered against classic findings. Negative scaphoid film. Negative nitrite. Negative Phalen. Normal creatinine in early nephropathy. A nonfocal neuro exam in brain abscess.A negative result lowers probability according to the test's performance. It supports ruling out disease only when the remaining probability is sufficiently low for the decision.
Unchecked attributeThe right category is retrieved and then never checked against the one attribute that separates its members – direction, age, duration, grade, timing, or kind. The option is the correct disease family with the wrong value on the deciding axis.Name the attribute the stem specified, out loud, before choosing: which direction, at what age, over how long, at which grade.
Class-vs-memberThe right drug class represented by the wrong member, making a keyed answer look like it contradicts a guideline. "NSAIDs are first-line for OA" – but the only NSAID offered is ketorolac, a 5-day drug, so acetaminophen wins.Read which specific agent represents each class before rejecting the class.
The recurring failure mode Fast-and-wrong misses cluster where the deciding fact is in the background – the past medical history, the gestational age, the menopausal status, the duration – rather than in the foreground finding. Recognition speed is not the problem; the missing step is a deliberate 10-second completion pass: read the entire lab panel and the entire PMH before locking.
